data.title: Fluconazole
data.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Triazole antifungal (first generation)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-α-demethylase (CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis
- Fungistatic; membrane damage from accumulated toxic methylated sterols

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble; about 90% bioavailable; absorption not affected by food or gastric acid
- Low protein binding; excellent CSF, eye and urine penetration
- Half-life about 30 h → weekly dosing possible
- Excreted unchanged in urine — reduce dose in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Vulvovaginal, oropharyngeal and oesophageal candidiasis; candidal intertrigo and paronychia
- Pityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis
- Dermatophytosis and onychomycosis (alternative)
- Cryptococcosis (including meningitis, with amphotericin B first), coccidioidomycosis
- Prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients

## Dose & formulations
- Vulvovaginal candidiasis: 150 mg single dose; recurrent: 150 mg every 72 h × 3 doses, then weekly for 6 months
- Oropharyngeal candidiasis: 100–200 mg/day × 7–14 days
- Tinea corporis: 150–300 mg once weekly × 2–4 weeks
- Pityriasis versicolor: 300 mg weekly × 2 weeks (or 400 mg single dose)
- Onychomycosis: 150–450 mg once weekly for 6–12 months
- Children: 3–6 mg/kg/day (tinea capitis 6 mg/kg/day)

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache
- Hepatotoxicity (usually mild)
- QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
- Alopecia with prolonged high doses
- Rash; fixed drug eruption (common in Indian practice); rarely SJS/TEN

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to azoles
- With QT-prolonging drugs metabolised by CYP3A4 (e.g. cisapride, pimozide, quinidine, erythromycin)
- Pregnancy (high-dose or prolonged use)

## Drug interactions
- Inhibits CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and (moderately) CYP3A4
- Raises levels of warfarin, phenytoin, sulfonylureas, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, some statins, benzodiazepines
- Rifampicin lowers fluconazole levels

## Monitoring
- LFT for courses longer than a few weeks; ECG if other QT risks; renal function for dosing

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid. High-dose or prolonged use in the first trimester is linked to birth defects (old FDA category D); a single 150 mg dose was category C. Compatible with breastfeeding in usual doses.

## Viva points
- Water-soluble azole — best CSF penetration, renal excretion
- Absorption is not acid-dependent (unlike itraconazole)
- Main enzyme inhibited for interactions: CYP2C9 (warfarin, phenytoin)
- Weekly dosing is possible because of the long half-life

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
